extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (training on 2019 PEG)
extracted.subtask_description: Apply the 2019 Patent Eligibility Guidance (PEG) framework (Step 1, Step 2A Prong One, Step 2A Prong Two, Step 2B) to determine whether a claim is directed to a judicial exception and whether additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application or provide an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1: statutory category
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate Step 1: Does this claim fall within a statutory category?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim recites a series of steps it is a process (Step 1 = Yes). Example: "The claim recites a series of steps and, therefore, is a process."

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One: identify abstract idea and grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Identify the specific limitation(s) in the claim that you believe recites an abstract idea; (b) Determine whether the identified limitation(s) falls within at least one of the groupings of abstract ideas enumerated in the 2019 PEG.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the 2019 PEG groupings (mathematical concepts; mental processes; certain methods of organizing human activity) to categorize the identified limitation. Example: the "encoding" step was identified as reciting mathematical concepts because it explicitly states formulas/calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2019 PEG grouping — Mathematical concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical concepts include mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, and mathematical calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim step explicitly uses formulas/calculations (e.g., CA = MA^e (mod n)), treat it as a mathematical concept under Step 2A Prong One. The example finds the encoding step recites mathematical concepts because the claim explicitly states the mathematical relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2019 PEG grouping — Mental processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental processes are concepts performed in the human mind (including an observation, evaluation, judgment, opinion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim element that, under its broadest reasonable interpretation, can be practically performed in the human mind is a mental process. Mere recitation of generic computer components (e.g., "by the network appliance") does not remove the limitation from the mental processes grouping. Example: a "comparing" step was found to be a mental process because it could be performed mentally absent more specific technological limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2019 PEG grouping — Certain methods of organizing human activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes fundamental economic principles or practices (e.g., hedging, insurance, mitigating risk), commercial or legal interactions (contracts, legal obligations, advertising/marketing/sales activities), and managing personal behavior/relationships or interactions between people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this grouping when the claimed concept is essentially an organizational/human-activity method. The guidance lists these categories for mapping claim limitations under Step 2A Prong One.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two: meaningful limit / practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether additional element(s) or a combination of elements in the claim apply, rely on, or use the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception, such that it is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for additional elements or specific combinations that integrate the judicial exception into a practical application or provide a specific technological improvement (e.g., collecting NetFlow data only when abnormal to avoid excess traffic and improve network monitoring). If the claim as a whole integrates the mental process into a practical application, Step 2A = No (not directed to abstract idea).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity (Prong Two anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional elements that are merely pre- or post-solution activity or general data gathering are insignificant extra-solution activity and do not meaningfully limit the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: reciting a collecting step at a high level of generality (gathering network delay, packet loss, jitter) amounts to mere data gathering; reciting a generic network appliance automating a comparison is merely instructing application of the exception on a generic computer. Such elements do not integrate the abstract idea into a practical application under Step 2A Prong Two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination must impose meaningful limits, not merely automate
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in combination, additional elements that amount to mere instructions to apply the exception using a generic computer component do not impose meaningful limits on practicing the abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The combination of collecting specified data and using a generic network appliance to perform comparisons was found insufficient because it only automates the exception and fails to impose meaningful limits on it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-as-a-whole analysis versus individual-step analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claim as a whole is directed to a particular improvement rather than relying solely on the analysis of individual steps, which may each appear to be pre- or post-solution activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: although individual collecting steps may be mere pre/post-solution activity, the claim as a whole could be directed to a particular improvement in collecting traffic data (e.g., reducing excess network traffic), and thus integrate the mental process into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B: inventive concept / "significantly more"
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate Step 2B: Does the claim provide an inventive concept, i.e., does the claim recite additional element(s) or a combination of elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception in the claim?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere instructions to apply an exception on a generic computer cannot provide an inventive concept. Determine whether additional elements are more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity in the field. If not, the claim remains ineligible (Step 2B = No).

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-evaluation in Step 2B for well-understood, routine, conventional (Berkheimer consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: A conclusion that an additional element is insignificant extra-solution activity in Step 2A should be re-evaluated in Step 2B to determine if that element is well-understood, routine, conventional in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use background evidence to determine conventionality. Example: if the background indicates the network appliance is an off-the-shelf generic computer and case law (Symantec, TLI, OIP Techs.) supports that mere collection over a network is conventional, then the additional element is well-understood/routine and does not supply an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recitation of generic computer components is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere nominal recitation of a generic computer or network appliance does not take a claim limitation out of a judicial exception (e.g., mental processes) nor does it supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: adding "by the network appliance" without more specific technical detail still allows the limitation to be performed in the mind or be considered generic automation; does not meaningfully limit or provide 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: When a combination of additional elements can make the claim eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: If the combination of additional elements uses the judicial exception in a meaningful way beyond generally linking it to a technological environment, and sufficiently limits the use of the judicial exception to a practical application, the claim may be more than a drafting effort to monopolize the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the cryptography example — the combination of receiving, transforming, encoding (with explicit mathematical formulas) and transmitting the ciphertext to a computer terminal over a communication channel was found to use mathematical concepts in a specific manner that limits the use of the mathematical concepts to the practical application, supporting eligibility under Step 2A Prong Two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting a rejection for an ineligible claim
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is ineligible, the rejection should identify the abstract idea, identify the additional elements and explain why they do not integrate the abstract idea into a practical application, and explain why the additional elements do not provide an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a reference to the appropriate enumerated grouping of abstract ideas. Use the new form paragraphs created for use with the 2019 PEG; a sample rejection is posted on the microsite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping claim limitations to example analyses (exemplar guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the provided examples to guide mapping of specific claim language to PEG groupings and Prong Two/Step 2B conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate subtleties: explicitly recited mathematical relations (encoding) -> mathematical concept; a transformation recited without explicit formulas may not be an abstract idea and may not be performable in the mind; collecting data 'when abnormal' that reduces network load -> specific technical improvement. Use these patterns when analyzing real claims.
